sections.title: The blue team and the security operations centre

blocks.title: About this page
blocks.text: Written for this site as of November 2026 for a fresher. Standards and tools change (OWASP Top 10 editions, TLS versions, certificate exams), so check the official source named in the text before relying on a detail. Practise only on systems you own or have written permission to test.

The **blue team** defends: it prevents what it can, detects what gets through and responds when something goes wrong. Most entry-level jobs are on this side. A **SOC (security operations centre)** is the team and the tooling that watch systems around the clock.

| Level | Typical work |
|---|---|
| **Tier 1 analyst** | watch the alert queue, triage (is it real?), close false positives, escalate real ones |
| **Tier 2 analyst** | investigate escalated incidents, scope the damage, contain, write the report |
| **Tier 3 / threat hunter** | proactively search for attackers that alerts missed, build detections, analyse malware |
| **SOC engineer / detection engineer** | build and tune the pipelines and rules |
| **Incident commander** | coordinates a major incident across teams |

Two numbers every SOC reports: **MTTD** (mean time to detect) and **MTTR** (mean time to respond or recover). Attackers who stay hidden for weeks are far more costly than ones caught in hours.

You cannot defend what you cannot see. Useful sources:

| Source | Tells you |
|---|---|
| **Authentication logs** (Linux `auth.log`, Windows Security log, identity provider) | who logged in, from where, how often they failed |
| **Web server and application logs** | requests, status codes, user agents, errors |
| **Firewall and network flow logs** | which hosts talk to which, on which ports, how much data |
| **DNS logs** | which names were looked up (malware beaconing, tunnelling) |
| **Endpoint (EDR) telemetry** | processes started, files written, registry changes |
| **Cloud audit logs** (AWS CloudTrail, GuardDuty) | who called which API, who changed an IAM policy |
| **Email gateway** | phishing attempts, attachments, sender checks |

A good log line has **time (with time zone), source, user, action, object and outcome**. Clocks must be synchronised (NTP) or events cannot be ordered. Logs should be **shipped to a central store** and protected from tampering.

### Windows event IDs you should recognise

| ID | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **4624** | successful logon |
| **4625** | failed logon |
| **4672** | special privileges assigned to a new logon (an administrator logged in) |
| **4688** | a new process was created |
| **4720** | a user account was created |
| **4732** | a member was added to a security-enabled local group |
| **1102** | the Security audit log was cleared (very suspicious) |
| **7045** | a new service was installed |

### Reading a web access log

blocks.title: One line of an access log (Common Log Format)

blocks.text: Clues: a `UNION SELECT` inside the query, the user agent `sqlmap`, and a **200** response (the request worked, which is worse than a 400 or 500). Typical triage commands:

blocks.code:
awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head          # top client IPs
awk '$9 ~ /^(401|403)/ {print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr   # who gets denied most
grep -iE "union(%20|\+| )select|<script|\.\./" access.log | head          # obvious attack strings
blocks.title: Find the noisiest sources and the failures

blocks.text:
- **401/403 floods from one IP** → brute force or forced browsing. **404 floods** → scanning. **500s after odd input** → injection attempts.
- **200 on a suspicious request** is the one to escalate, because it may have succeeded.
- **Windows:** 4625 many times then 4624 for the same account = a brute force that worked.
- **Linux:** `Failed password` lines followed by `Accepted password` from the same IP = the same story.
- **4688 plus an unusual parent** (Word starting PowerShell) = classic malicious macro.
- **Event 1102 / log cleared** = the attacker is covering tracks.
blocks.title: Log analysis cheat codes

sections.title: Detection: SIEM, rules and alert quality

blocks.text:
A **SIEM** (security information and event management: Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, Elastic Security, Wazuh) collects logs from everywhere, normalises them, stores them and runs **correlation rules** that turn raw events into alerts.

Examples of useful detections:

| Detection | Logic |
|---|---|
| **Brute force** | more than 10 failed logins for one account or from one IP in 5 minutes |
| **Successful login after many failures** | 4625 × N followed by 4624 for the same user |
| **Impossible travel** | the same user logs in from two countries within minutes |
| **New administrator** | a user is added to a privileged group outside change windows |
| **Mass download / exfiltration** | one account reads far more data than its baseline |
| **Beaconing** | an internal host contacts one external address at fixed intervals |
| **Persistence** | a new scheduled task, service or autorun entry |

Rules can be written in a portable format called **Sigma** and translated to each SIEM's query language.

### Alert outcomes and quality

| | The activity is really malicious | The activity is benign |
|---|---|---|
| **Alert fires** | **True positive (TP)** | **False positive (FP)** |
| **No alert** | **False negative (FN)**: the dangerous miss | **True negative (TN)** |

- **Precision** = TP / (TP + FP): of the alerts, how many were real. **Recall** (detection rate) = TP / (TP + FN): of the real attacks, how many were caught.
- Too many false positives cause **alert fatigue**: analysts start ignoring alerts, and the real one gets missed. Tune rules, add context (asset criticality, user role), and automate the routine triage (**SOAR**).
- **Baselines** (what is normal for this user and host) make anomaly detection possible but need care.

Other detection tools: **IDS/IPS** (Snort, Suricata) on the network, **EDR** (endpoint detection and response) on hosts, **honeypots** and **canary tokens** (a fake credential or file that alerts when touched), and **threat hunting** (a human searching a hypothesis such as "has any server beaconed to a rare domain?").

### Threat intelligence

**Indicators of compromise (IOCs)** are artefacts of an attack: IP addresses, domains, file hashes, URLs. They are easy to share but attackers change them quickly. **TTPs** (tactics, techniques and procedures, as in MITRE ATT&CK) describe behaviour and are much harder to change, so they are more valuable. Sources: MISP, AlienVault OTX, VirusTotal, CISA advisories, vendor reports. Look up a suspicious file by its **hash**, not by uploading sensitive files to public services.

### Analysing a suspicious email

1. Look at the **headers**, not just the display name: `From`, `Return-Path`, `Reply-To`, `Received` chain.
2. Check authentication results:

| Mechanism | What it does |
|---|---|
| **SPF** | a DNS record listing the servers allowed to send mail for a domain |
| **DKIM** | the sending server signs the message; the receiver verifies it with a key published in DNS |
| **DMARC** | a policy (`none`, `quarantine`, `reject`) telling receivers what to do when SPF or DKIM fail to align with the visible From domain, and where to send reports |

3. Hover over links (do not click). Look for look-alike domains (`rn` instead of `m`), URL shorteners, mismatched display text.
4. Detonate attachments and links **only** in a sandbox, never on your own machine.
5. Search the mail system for other recipients and remove the message from all inboxes. If anyone clicked, treat their account as compromised: reset credentials, revoke sessions, check for mailbox rules.

### Static and dynamic malware analysis

- **Static analysis** inspects the file without running it: hash it, read strings, check imports and file type.
- **Dynamic analysis** runs it in an isolated **sandbox** and watches processes, files, registry and network traffic.
- Never analyse live malware on a machine connected to your network or your accounts.

An **incident** is an event that harms or threatens confidentiality, integrity or availability. NIST SP 800-61 and the SANS model describe the same lifecycle:

| Phase | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1. Preparation** | policies, contact lists, playbooks, tools, backups, training, tabletop exercises |
| **2. Detection and analysis** (identification) | decide whether it is an incident, scope it, rate severity, start a timeline |
| **3. Containment** | stop the spread: isolate hosts, disable accounts, block IPs. Short-term first, then long-term |
| **4. Eradication** | remove the cause: malware, backdoors, the vulnerability that let them in |
| **5. Recovery** | restore from clean backups, monitor closely, return to normal |
| **6. Lessons learned** | a blameless review within days: what worked, what failed, what to change |

Principles during an incident:

- **Contain before you clean.** Isolating a machine (network, not power) keeps evidence in memory.
- **Preserve evidence** following the **order of volatility** (most volatile first): CPU registers and cache → **memory (RAM)** → network connections and running processes → disk → remote logs and backups → archives. Record who handled what and when (**chain of custody**) and work on copies.
- **Keep a timeline and write things down.** Decisions made at 3 a.m. need to be explained at 10 a.m.
- **Communicate:** a named incident lead, a separate channel for the response team, careful statements for management, legal and customers. Know your legal reporting duties (for example, CERT-In reporting in India).
- **Do not pay** a ransom without legal and executive involvement. Restoration from tested backups is the plan.

### Three mini playbooks

| Incident | First steps |
|---|---|
| **Compromised account** | reset the password, revoke sessions and tokens, require MFA, review the sign-in history and mailbox rules, find what the account accessed |
| **Ransomware** | isolate affected hosts and shares, protect backups, identify the strain and the entry point, notify, restore from clean backups, patch the entry |
| **Web application attack** | preserve logs, block the source, find the vulnerable endpoint, patch, rotate secrets that may have been read, check for web shells |

- **CVE** gives a vulnerability a public ID (CVE-2021-44228). **CWE** classifies the weakness type (CWE-89 SQL injection). **CVSS** scores severity from 0 to 10 (Low, Medium, High, Critical). **EPSS** estimates the probability that a CVE will be exploited soon. CISA's **KEV catalogue** lists vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild.
- **Prioritise** by exploitability (is there a public exploit? is it in KEV?), **exposure** (internet-facing?) and **asset value**. A medium-scored flaw on an exposed, exploited system can outrank a critical one on an isolated test box.
- **Patch cadence:** critical and exploited issues in days, others on a regular cycle. If you cannot patch, use compensating controls (segmentation, a WAF rule, disabling the feature).
- **Scanners** (Nessus, OpenVAS, Qualys, Trivy for containers) find known issues. They miss logic flaws and they report false positives, so verify.

**Backups** are the last line of defence against ransomware. Follow **3-2-1**: three copies of the data, on two different media, with one offsite. Add an **immutable** or offline copy and **test restores** regularly. **RPO** (recovery point objective) is how much data loss is acceptable, **RTO** (recovery time objective) is how long recovery may take. A **business continuity plan** keeps the business running and a **disaster recovery plan** restores IT.

### Frameworks you will hear about

| Framework | Use |
|---|---|
| **NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0** | six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover |
| **CIS Controls** | a prioritised list of practical safeguards |
| **ISO/IEC 27001** | a certifiable information security management system |
| **PCI DSS** | rules for organisations that handle payment card data |
| **MITRE ATT&CK** | a library of attacker behaviour for detection and testing |

"First check the context: which account, which source, how many, over what time, and what the system is. Then look for a success afterwards for the same account or source. If there is none, check whether the source is a known scanner or user error. If there is a success, treat the account as compromised: reset credentials, kill sessions, look at what it did, escalate. Document the steps, and tune the rule or add the source to a watchlist if it was benign."
blocks.title: Walk me through an alert about many failed logins
Key points
blocks.text:
- Logs from authentication, web, network, DNS, endpoint and cloud are what detection is built from
- A false negative is the dangerous miss and too many false positives cause alert fatigue
- Incident response runs prepare, detect and analyse, contain, eradicate, recover, learn
- Contain before you clean and preserve volatile evidence first
- Prioritise patching by exploitability, exposure and asset value, not CVSS alone
- Backups need three copies, two media, one offsite and tested restores

50 original questions on 11 areas. *Recall* questions test a definition or a rule. *Scenario* questions give you a situation, a log or a snippet and ask what is wrong or what to do. Pick an answer to see why it is right and which trap catches people.

items.q: *(Recall)* A Tier 1 SOC analyst's main job is to
o: triage alerts, close false positives and escalate real incidents
items.w: Tier 1 watches the queue, decides what is real and hands real incidents to deeper investigation.

items.q: *(Recall)* MTTD stands for
items.w: It measures how long attackers go unnoticed. Shorter is better, as is MTTR (time to respond or recover).

items.q: *(Recall)* Why must the clocks of all servers be synchronised (NTP) for incident investigation?
o: events from different systems can only be ordered into a timeline if their timestamps agree
items.w: Without consistent time, correlating a firewall event with a login event is guesswork.

items.q: *(Recall)* Windows Security event ID 4625 means
items.w: 4624 is success, 4625 is failure, 7045 is a new service, 1102 is a cleared audit log.

items.q: *(Recall)* Windows Security event ID 1102 (audit log cleared) is suspicious because
o: it means the disk is full
it is a normal daily event
attackers clear logs to cover their tracks
items.w: Log clearing outside planned maintenance is a strong sign of intrusion.

items.q: *(Recall)* Event ID 4688 records
o: the creation of a new process
items.w: Process creation logs, with the command line enabled, are one of the best sources for detecting malicious activity.

items.q: *(Scenario)* Which sequence in an authentication log most strongly suggests a successful brute force?
o: many 4625 events for an account from one IP, followed by a 4624 for the same account from that IP
items.w: Failures followed by a success from the same source mean the guess eventually worked.

items.q: *(Scenario)* You see `Failed password for root from 198.51.100.7` 400 times, then `Accepted password for root from 198.51.100.7`. The first action is to
o: treat the host as compromised: isolate it, preserve evidence and investigate what root did afterwards
ignore it because root exists on every server
items.w: A success after a flood of failures means the attacker got in. Containment and evidence come first.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A web access log shows a request containing UNION SELECT and a 200 status with a large response size, from user agent sqlmap. What is the most important observation?
o: the 200 and large response suggest the injection may have succeeded and data may have been returned
items.w: Attempts that return errors are noise. A 200 with unusual size on an injection attempt needs urgent investigation.

items.q:
*(Scenario)* Given this log excerpt, which IP made the most requests?
```text
10.0.0.5 GET /
10.0.0.9 GET /login
10.0.0.9 POST /login
10.0.0.9 POST /login
10.0.0.5 GET /about
10.0.0.9 POST /login
```
items.w: 10.0.0.9 appears four times (one GET and three POSTs to /login), against twice for 10.0.0.5. Repeated POSTs to /login from one address suggest password guessing.

items.q: *(Scenario)* How many POST /login requests are in the excerpt above?
items.w: Lines 3, 4 and 6 are POST /login.

items.q: *(Recall)* A burst of HTTP 404 responses to many different paths from a single IP most likely indicates
items.w: Scanners probe many URLs looking for hidden files and admin pages.

items.q: *(Recall)* A SIEM is used to
o: collect, normalise and correlate logs from many sources and raise alerts
items.w: Examples: Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, Elastic Security, Wazuh.

items.q: *(Recall)* Sigma is
o: a vendor-neutral format for writing detection rules
items.w: A Sigma rule can be converted to the query language of different SIEMs.

items.q: *(Recall)* "Impossible travel" detection raises an alert when
o: a user logs in at night
the same account signs in from two distant locations too quickly for physical travel
items.w: It may indicate stolen credentials, though VPNs can cause false positives.

items.q: *(Scenario)* An organisation has an alert rule for "failed logins > 3 in 10 minutes" and receives 500 alerts a day, mostly users who mistyped passwords. The best improvement is
o: tune it: raise the threshold, add context such as source reputation and success afterwards, and automate the routine triage
items.w: Alert fatigue hides real attacks. Better rules and automation raise the signal-to-noise ratio.

items.q: *(Recall)* A real attack that produces no alert is a
items.w: False negatives are the most dangerous failures of a detection system.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A rule fired 100 times: 80 were real attacks and 20 were benign. The precision is
items.w: Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 80 / 100 = 80%.

items.q: *(Scenario)* During a month there were 50 real attacks. The rule caught 40 of them. The recall (detection rate) is
items.w: Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 40 / 50 = 80%. Ten attacks were missed.

items.q: *(Scenario)* Tuning a rule to remove all false positives made it miss several real attacks. Which statement describes the trade-off?
o: making a rule stricter tends to raise precision but can reduce recall
items.w: Detection engineering balances noisy alerts against missed attacks. Measure both.

items.q: *(Recall)* Which indicator is hardest for an attacker to change?
items.w: Changing a hash or IP is trivial. Changing how the attack works is expensive, which is why ATT&CK techniques are valuable detection targets.

items.q: *(Recall)* An IOC (indicator of compromise) is
o: an artefact such as an IP, domain or file hash associated with malicious activity
items.w: IOCs are shared quickly but become stale quickly.

items.q: *(Recall)* A canary token is
o: a decoy credential, file or URL that raises an alert when someone touches it
items.w: It is cheap and has a very low false-positive rate: legitimate users never touch it.

items.q: *(Recall)* An SPF record lists
o: the servers allowed to send e-mail for the domain
items.w: The receiving server compares the sending IP with the domain's SPF record.

items.q: *(Recall)* DKIM provides
o: a digital signature on the message that the receiver verifies with a public key in DNS
items.w: It shows the message was authorised by the signing domain and was not altered.

items.q: *(Recall)* A DMARC policy of p=reject tells receivers to
o: reject messages that fail the aligned SPF/DKIM checks
items.w: It protects the domain from being spoofed in the From header. p=none only reports.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A message claims to be from "IT Support" but the Return-Path domain is a look-alike (examp1e.com) and SPF fails. The best action is to
o: reply asking if it is real
click the link to test it
report it, search for and remove the same message from other mailboxes, and block the domain
items.w: Triage by headers, contain the campaign by removing copies, and check whether anyone clicked.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A user clicked a link in a phishing email and typed their password. What should be done?
o: reset the password, revoke sessions and tokens, review sign-in logs and mailbox rules, and check for lateral activity
items.w: Assume the credentials are in the attacker's hands. Mailbox forwarding rules are a common persistence trick.

items.q: *(Recall)* Static malware analysis means
o: examining the file without executing it, for example hashes, strings and imports
items.w: Dynamic analysis runs it in a sandbox and observes behaviour.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A suspicious attachment arrives. The safest way to learn what it does is to
o: analyse it in an isolated sandbox with no connection to your network
items.w: Live malware must be contained. Hash lookups on reputation services are the safe first step.

items.q: *(Recall)* The first phase of the incident response lifecycle is
items.w: Playbooks, tools, contacts and training must exist before the incident.

items.q: *(Recall)* After detecting that a workstation is infected, the first priority is usually
o: contain it by isolating it from the network while preserving evidence
turn off the whole data centre
items.w: Containment stops the spread. Cleaning too early destroys evidence and leaves the root cause unknown.

items.q: *(Scenario)* Why isolate a suspected compromised host from the network instead of powering it off?
o: powering off loses volatile evidence in memory, such as running processes and connections
items.w: RAM contents disappear at shutdown. Isolation stops the attacker's access while keeping evidence.

items.q: *(Scenario)* Which list is in the correct order of volatility, most volatile first?
o: registers and cache, RAM, network connections and processes, disk, remote logs and backups
items.w: Collect the data that disappears fastest first.

items.q: *(Recall)* Chain of custody documents
o: who handled evidence, when and what they did, so it stays trustworthy
items.w: Without it, evidence may be challenged in disciplinary or legal proceedings.

items.q: *(Recall)* The purpose of a blameless post-incident review is to
o: learn what happened and improve controls and processes
items.w: Blame discourages people from reporting problems early.

items.q: *(Scenario)* Ransomware encrypts file servers. Backups exist on a share that is mounted on the same servers. What is the likely problem?
o: the backups were reachable and may also be encrypted; keep an offline or immutable copy
items.w: That is why the 3-2-1 rule includes an offsite or offline copy, and why restore tests matter.

items.q: *(Recall)* An RPO of 4 hours means
o: up to 4 hours of data may be lost
items.w: RPO is about data loss. RTO is about recovery time.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A business requires that after a failure the system is back within 2 hours with at most 15 minutes of data lost. Which is correct?
items.w: Time to restore is RTO, tolerable data loss is RPO.

items.q: *(Recall)* The 3-2-1 backup rule is
items.w: Add an immutable or offline copy and test restores regularly.

items.q: *(Recall)* CWE-89 refers to
items.w: CWE classifies weakness types. A CVE identifies one specific vulnerability in a product.

items.q: *(Recall)* CISA's KEV catalogue lists
o: vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild
items.w: Presence in KEV is a strong signal to patch urgently.

items.q: *(Scenario)* Which vulnerability should usually be fixed first?
o: CVSS 9.0 in an unused library function
CVSS 7.5 on an internet-facing server with a public exploit being used in attacks
CVSS 9.8 on an isolated, offline test machine
items.w: Prioritise by exploitation, exposure and asset value, using CVSS as one input.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A scanner reports a critical flaw on a legacy device that cannot be patched. A good response is
o: apply compensating controls such as network isolation, access restrictions and monitoring, and record the risk acceptance
items.w: When patching is impossible, reduce exposure and document the decision.

items.q: *(Recall)* EPSS is a score that estimates
o: the probability that a vulnerability will be exploited in the near future
items.w: It complements CVSS, which measures severity rather than likelihood.

items.q: *(Recall)* The NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 added which function to the original five?
items.w: CSF 2.0 has Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.

items.q: *(Recall)* MITRE ATT&CK is
o: a knowledge base of real attacker tactics and techniques
items.w: Used to map detections, plan red-team exercises and discuss incidents.

items.q: *(Recall)* ISO/IEC 27001 is
o: a certifiable standard for an information security management system
items.w: Organisations are audited against it by an accredited certification body.

items.q: *(Scenario)* A user reports that their mailbox is forwarding all mail to an unknown address and they never set it up. This most likely means
o: the account was compromised and an attacker created a forwarding rule for persistence
items.w: Mailbox rules are a classic persistence and data-theft technique after account takeover.

items.q: *(Scenario)* On a web server you find a file `uploads/img.php` containing a few lines that run commands from a request parameter. This is a
o: web shell, a sign of compromise
items.w: A web shell gives the attacker remote command execution. Preserve evidence, find the entry point, rotate secrets and rebuild from a clean image.

items.question: What is the difference between a false positive and a false negative, and which is worse for security?
items.answer: A false positive is an alert on benign activity. A false negative is a real attack with no alert. The false negative is worse because the attack goes unnoticed, although too many false positives hide real alerts.

items.question: You see Windows events 4625 repeatedly for one account followed by 4624 from the same IP. What do you conclude?
items.answer: A brute force attack that probably succeeded. Treat the account as compromised: reset it, kill sessions and investigate what it accessed.

items.question: Why is the order of volatility important?
items.answer: Evidence in memory and network state disappears when a machine is powered off or rebooted, so it must be captured before the more permanent disk and log evidence.

items.question: Explain SPF, DKIM and DMARC in one sentence each.
items.answer: SPF lists which servers may send for a domain. DKIM signs messages so the receiver can verify them. DMARC sets the policy for failures and ties the checks to the visible From domain.

items.question: What does 3-2-1 mean for backups and why test restores?
items.answer: Three copies, on two media types, one offsite. A backup you have never restored may be corrupt, incomplete or too slow to meet the recovery time objective.

items.question: A CVSS 9.8 flaw exists on an isolated lab server and a CVSS 6.5 flaw is on a public web server listed in the KEV catalogue. Which is patched first?
items.answer: Usually the 6.5 flaw on the exposed, actively exploited system. Prioritisation uses exploitation, exposure and asset value, not the score alone.
